$comment: Pinned reference measurements for LexiSharp.Eval. Two kinds of assertion live here and they are
regression pins  — the value LexiSharp produces at a fixed configuration. Tight tolerance.
These are the teeth of the net: deterministic, and they catch any change to
scoring, candidate generation, tokenization or metrics.
parity figures   — the independent implementation's number for the same task and index.
A credibility claim with a source, not a guard. |lexisharp - anserini| is
meaningful only where the configuration is genuinely aligned, and the
arguana row is aligned across different BM25 parameters, which is recorded
as such rather than glossed over.
Run --verify-reference to see what moved, then edit expectedNdcg here by hand: --write is
accepted and writes nothing, deliberately. Read the diff before committing it: re-recording is
how a pinned baseline stops catching anything.

Re-recorded from 0.289 to 0.3195 when the pin began to replay the table's query syntax instead of inheriting the library default: SearchOptions.ParseQuerySyntax defaults to true (a double quote is a phrase delimiter), and the pin used to replay that while the table this row is compared against runs literal-text queries. On ArguAna 146 of 1,406 test queries carry a double quote, so the difference is 0.030 nDCG — not a regression, a configuration the pin no longer misnames. The parity figure 0.3970 is unaffected, being measured on a run the table itself wrote under the same convention.

RE-RECORDED after a fix, and the value it replaces recorded a defect rather than a behaviour. SearchOptions.ExcludedDocumentIds was never applied on the term-at-a-time path, which is the one this query takes on a corpus of 8,674 documents and 645-word queries, so the document being excluded stayed at rank 1 - and for this corpus it is the lexically closest document to the query, because the query text is a document's own text. 0.2864 is what the option produced while doing nothing. Measured after the fix: 0.3806, now 0.4180 — re-recorded together with the other ArguAna pins when the gate began to replay the table's literal-text queries: the fix measurement above inherited library query syntax (a double quote is a phrase), while the table this row is compared against treats quotes as prose, so the fix now reads higher. The other nDCG pins and all three index fingerprints are unchanged and the golden master is byte-identical, which is the evidence that the fix reached the path it was aimed at and no other. The same config also publishes recall, which this harness measures but the pin does not yet assert: reference R@100 0.9324, R@1000 0.9872, at k1=0.9, b=0.4. Not asserted here because the pinned metric is nDCG@10 and the recall figures are recorded in the configuration's own results block for a reader who wants them.

The alignment row, measured with the reference's own conventions: its analyzer (uax29, which keeps an apostrophe inside a word), k1=0.9/b=0.4, linear gains, the repeated query term counted once per occurrence, its index statistics (average over non-empty documents, one-byte length quantisation), its four-decimal score rounding, the omitted saturation constant and single-precision arithmetic. Under those the figure matches the published one to the fourth decimal, and the index fingerprint agrees to 0.1% (NFCorpus) and 0.0% (SciFact) rather than the 2.8%/1.5% the English analyzer leaves.

The alignment row for ArguAna, under the reference's conventions: uax29, k1=0.9/b=0.4, linear gains, the repeated-term rule, the query document excluded, and the four arithmetic options. It reads 0.4005 against the published 0.3970 - a gap of 0.0035 that is not reproduced by the configuration the parity row named. The 0.3970 that row carried was not what this configuration measures; it is withdrawn, and this pin is what the documented command produces.

The configuration of this library that lands closest to the 2021 paper's 0.325 on NFCorpus: uax29, k1=1.2/b=0.75, distinct terms, no exclusion, exponential gains. 0.324 - a difference of 0.001, and it is a different configuration from the one that lands on SciFact or ArguAna.

The highest nDCG@10 observed on NFCorpus among the configurations tried (uax29; k1 0.9-3.0; b 0.3-1.0; distinct terms; no exclusion; exponential gains). In-sample: the grid was chosen on the same 323 queries it is scored on, so this is an upper bound, not a result.

The highest nDCG@10 observed on SciFact among the configurations tried. In-sample upper bound, same grid as nfcorpus/best-observed. The closest to the paper's 0.665 is the scifact/default pin at 0.662.

The configuration of this library that lands on the 2021 paper's 0.315 for ArguAna: uax29, k1=1.5/b=0.75, distinct terms, no exclusion, exponential gains. It reads 0.315 - the paper's figure exactly - with a configuration that is not the reference's (that one is at 0.9/0.4 and reads 0.4005 under exclusion).

The highest nDCG@10 observed on ArguAna among the configurations tried. In-sample upper bound. The reading rises with k1 across the grid and 3.0 is its edge, so the true maximum on a wider grid is not known and is not claimed.

indexFingerprints.note: The `english` analyzer, which is not the reference's: it splits contractions, folds diacritics and uses the library's separator set, so its index holds 2.8% more terms. The `uax29` pin for this corpus is the one that matches the reference (0.1%). Kept because every published table in this repository before the alignment fix was measured with `english`.

The `english` analyzer, which is not the reference's: it splits contractions, folds diacritics and uses the library's separator set, so its index holds 1.5% more terms. The `uax29` pin for this corpus is the one that matches the reference (0.005%). Kept because every published table in this repository before the alignment fix was measured with `english`.

The `english` analyzer against the reference's term count: 1.12% more terms. The cause is the analysis, not the corpus - the `uax29` analyzer brings the same comparison to 0.1% on NFCorpus and 0.005% on SciFact. Between the two analyzers the separator set, the diacritic folding, the possessive handling and the UAX#29 boundaries all differ; the earlier note here attributed the whole gap to contractions, and that was not decomposed.

The reference's tokenizer, including the two rules that closed the last gap: symbol tokens (© ® ™ ↔, which Lucene 10 emits and 4.8 dropped) and the middle dot joining two letters (mg·dl as one term). The count is the published one exactly, so the tolerance is zero - any drift here is a tokenizer change, not corpus noise.

parity.lexisharpConfig: nfcorpus/uax29-aligned at k1=0.9, b=0.4, reference conventions on
parity.note: Like for like: 0.3218 at the reference's own k1=0.9, b=0.4, under its analyzer (uax29: apostrophes inside a word, possessives stripped before the stop list), its linear gains, its repeated-term rule, its index statistics, its score rounding, its omitted saturation constant and its single precision - the configuration the ArguAna parity established. Against 0.3218 published: no difference. The 0.3215 this field carried before was measured with the `english` analyzer and without the arithmetic options; that analyzer's index holds 2.8% more terms than the reference's, and the agreement to the fourth decimal was a coincidence rather than a match.

parity.lexisharpConfig: scifact/uax29-aligned at k1=0.9, b=0.4, reference conventions on
parity.note: Like for like: 0.6789 at the reference's own k1=0.9, b=0.4, under its analyzer (uax29), its linear gains, its repeated-term rule, its index statistics, its score rounding, its omitted saturation constant and its single precision. Against 0.6789 published: no difference. The 0.6788 this field carried before was the `english` analyzer's distinct-term reading, and its fourth-decimal agreement was the coincidence that hid a 2.8%-larger index.

parity.lexisharpConfig: arguana/uax29-aligned at k1=0.9, b=0.4, reference conventions on
parity.reproducibilityNote: Measured today with the same third-party tool on a run written by this harness, and independently by this harness. trec_eval 9.0.8 reads ndcg_cut_10 0.3970 and recall_100 0.9324 on it, against 0.3970 and 0.9324 published; this harness reads 0.3970 on the same run. The two metrics are computed differently and agree to four decimals. With the reference's own scale, precision and post-processing - see --reference-score-rounding, --omit-saturation-constant, --single-precision-bm25 and --reference-index-statistics, all off by default - 15,466 of 15,466 compared (query, document) scores over all 1,406 queries match on the raw bits, so the ranking is the reference's ranking and not a lookalike. A residual 0.0004 between this harness and trec_eval on the rounded run is confined to 102 of 1,406 queries, every one containing a tie in the returned scores. A tie in the returned scores is the plausible mechanism, because it is the only property those 102 queries share, and it is not established: neither the order written in the run file, nor document id, nor a reversal of the tied group reproduces trec_eval's reading, and 93 of 183 fit a reversal. Which order produced the published figure is not established either, and is not claimed. The row is left at 0.397, which is what it now measures: re-recording a baseline is a reviewed act, and a value that was measured to land on the recorded one needs no edit.
parity.variants: uax29 + reference index statistics + parity options -> 0.3970. The 0.401 and 0.403 recorded earlier on this row were measured with the metrics taken at the run's retrieval depth rather than at rank 10: a parity run retrieves one document deeper than it measures, so --top-k 11 produced nDCG@11 under a heading reading nDCG@10. That 0.006 was the eleventh document. Fixed in Evaluation.cs as MetricDepth, and the aggregate is unaffected by it at the published depth.
parity.note: Like for like: 0.4005 at the reference's own k1=0.9, b=0.4, under its analyzer (uax29), its linear gains, its repeated-term rule, the query document excluded, its index statistics, score rounding, omitted saturation constant and single precision. Against 0.3970 published, a gap of 0.0035. The 0.3970 this row carried was not what the documented configuration measures - it is the published figure, and the parity section is displayed but never replayed, so nothing caught the difference. The bit-level score claim on this corpus is withdrawn with it.

referenceSource.what: The BM25 figures on the three corpora below, and the index statistics, are the ones Anserini's own BEIR reproduction configs record as the result of their 'bm25' model. They are not transcribed from a paper's table: the configs carry the numbers in a results block next to the command that produced them.
referenceSource.perCorpusConfig: beir-v1.0.0-{arguana,nfcorpus,scifact}.flat.yaml, one file per corpus, each carrying index_stats, the metric command, the model parameters and the results
referenceSource.analyzedIndex: BeirFlatCollection with DefaultLuceneDocumentGenerator: title and text concatenated into one field, as this harness does too
referenceSource.analysis: Lucene EnglishAnalyzer: Porter stemming, its 33-word stop list, single-character terms kept. StopWords.EnglishFunction is word-for-word that list, checked.
referenceSource.parameters: k1=0.9, b=0.4 - not an assumption. The configs pass '-bm25' with no override, and Anserini's own defaults for -bm25.k1 and -bm25.b are 0.9 and 0.4, chosen to follow Trotman et al. (SIGIR 2012 OSIR Workshop). Lucene's own BM25 defaults are 1.2/0.75, so this had to be checked rather than assumed.
referenceSource.queryOwnDocument: REMOVED. The configs pass '-removeQuery', documented as 'Remove docids that have the query id when writing final run output'. So the published ArguAna figure was produced with the query's own document dropped - which is the convention --exclude-query-doc implements, and the reason that gate was a defect here rather than a nicety: 1,298 of ArguAna's 1,406 test queries are corpus documents whose text is the query text.
referenceSource.verifiedOn: Every figure and index statistic above was read back out of the configs on readOn, not carried from an earlier session: 0.3970 / 0.3218 / 0.6789 and 8674/8673/969528, 3633/3633/637485, 5183/5183/838128.
referenceSource.docgenTemplate: beir-v1.0.0-{corpus}.flat.template, which states the index construction in its own words: "These experiments index the corpus in a 'flat' manner, by concatenating the 'title' and 'text' into the 'contents' field." This harness concatenates them the same way, checked rather than assumed.
referenceSource.theBaselineIsNotOneNumber: The 2021 BEIR paper reports BM25 on arguana at 0.315, and indexes the title and passage as SEPARATE text fields through Elasticsearch defaults. Anserini's regression reports 0.3970 for the same corpus at the same k1 and b, indexing title and text concatenated. The two published values are 0.082 apart because they are different indexes. nfcorpus and scifact agree across both, so the arguana row is the one where the choice of published figure changes the conclusion.
referenceSource.noPublishedRunFile: The reproduction directory publishes commands, configs and docgen only - no results, and no per-query trec_run. Attribution of the remaining arguana gap therefore needs that file from outside this repository; it is bounded and characterised here instead.
referenceSource.otherPublishedValues: BM25 on arguana has at least three published values, differing by construction: 0.315 (the 2021 BEIR paper, title and body as separate fields, Elasticsearch), 0.3970 (Anserini's flat regression, concatenated), 0.414 (the official BEIR leaderboard paper, Anserini multi-field with --fields contents=1.0 title=1.0). The spread is 0.099. This library measures 0.364 flat and 0.370 multi-field at the same k1 and b, both inside that spread, which is why a deficit against one of them is not by itself evidence of a defect. The multi-field figure was measured here by scoring the title and the body as separate fields with their own statistics and summing the scores.
